1. Core Clinical Tension: A 60-year-old male with pre-existing pulmonary fibrosis presents with new-onset generalized seizures and occipital headaches. Brain imaging (CT and MRI) reveals a calcified, hemorrhagic dural-associated frontal mass with prominent perilesional edema and mass effect, closely mimicking a central nervous system neoplasm such as a meningioma, rather than an infectious lesion.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission evaluation concludes following initial neuroimaging (brain CT and MRI) and presentation of focal neurological deficits, prior to neurosurgical tumor resection, histopathological examination of the operative specimen, and thoraco-abdominal staging scans.
3. Differential Distinctions: An intracranial meningioma or primary brain tumor typically presents as a solitary extra-axial or peripheral calcified mass with surrounding vasogenic edema in older adults. However, a cerebral tuberculoma can present identically as a calcified, pseudo-tumoral space-occupying lesion with mass effect and intralesional hemorrhage, which is definitively distinguished only by surgical histopathology revealing caseating granulomatous inflammation.
case_prompt:
A 60-year-old male with a significant past medical history of diffuse bilateral infiltrative pulmonary disease at the stage of fibrosis presented after experiencing two generalized tonic-clonic seizures accompanied by persistent occipital headaches. During clinical observation, he developed recurrent seizure episodes associated with progressive motor weakness and heaviness involving the right upper extremity.

Non-contrast computed tomography (CT) of the brain revealed a calcified left frontal lesion with marked surrounding vasogenic edema, concerning for an intracranial mass. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain confirmed a left posterior peripheral frontal mass demonstrating intralesional hemorrhage, substantial surrounding edema, and local mass effect exerting compression on the ipsilateral lateral ventricle, radiologically concerning for an intracranial neoplasm such as a meningioma.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Preoperative brain MRI demonstrated a peripheral frontal mass with intralesional hemorrhage and mass effect, radiologically mimicking a meningioma, but surgical excision and histopathology revealed granulomatous inflammation with caseous necrosis rather than meningothelial neoplasia.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Brain MRI showed a left posterior peripheral frontal meningioma with intralesional bleeding and significant edema around it with mass effect on the ipsilateral lateral ventricle.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Initial cranial CT suggested a calcified frontal tumor with surrounding edema, but histopathology following surgical resection excluded malignancy, identifying an infectious pseudo-tumor.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: CT scan showed a left frontal tumor, calcified lesion with edema around it.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Neurosurgical resection and pathological anatomical analysis demonstrated a cerebromeningeal granuloma with caseous necrosis presenting as a pseudo-tumor (tuberculoma), establishing the definitive diagnosis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Pathological anatomical examination of the surgical specimen found a cerebromeningeal Granuloma with caseous necrosis in its pseudo tumor presentation (tuberculoma).
